_readme: U6 — The perfect: linking an earlier event to a later moment. Eleven points, authored to the closed id list.
sequence_index values come from the private band 1400-1499 and are ordered so that every point follows everything it depends on. The renumbering pass reseats them into the final 1..154.
gr_past_participle is the convergence node feeding the perfect, the passive and the participle clauses, so its form coverage is deliberately complete.
gr_pp_vs_past_simple carries four twin pairs because it is the highest-traffic tense choice in the language.
gr_past_perfect_choice exists to kill decorative past perfect as much as to teach it.

points.title: Building the third form of a verb, the one that follows have and be

teach.can_do: I can build the third form of any verb and put it after have or after be.
teach.why_it_matters: Nine later points run on this one form. Get it wrong once and the error turns up in the perfect, in the passive and in every conditional you write.
teach.meaning: Every English verb has three forms and you learn them together. The first is the plain one a dictionary lists: drive. The second reports a finished past event all by itself: drove. The third cannot stand alone at all. It waits for a helper, and then does two very different jobs: after have it builds the perfect, and after be it builds the passive. On its own it carries no time and no person.

form.pattern: regular: verb + -ed. irregular: a third form learned alongside the other two, as in drive / drove / driven
notes: Regular spelling: add -d after a silent e (close, closed); -y becomes -ied after a consonant (carry, carried); a final consonant doubles after one stressed vowel (plan, planned)
Irregular verbs fall into three families: all three forms alike (cut, cut, cut); the last two alike (build, built, built); all three different (write, wrote, written)
The form never changes for person, number or time. Every one of those jobs belongs to the helper standing in front of it
After have it means the perfect: they have built it. After be it means the passive: it was built
form.negative: The third form is never negated itself. Not attaches to the helper: has not built, was not built.
form.question: The helper moves to the front and the third form stays where it is: Has the crossing been rebuilt?

spec.label: the three forms every English verb has

steps.gloss: the plain form: dictionaries, after to, after a modal
the past simple: it can be the whole verb on its own
the third form: it needs have or be standing in front of it

worked_example.sentence: The Sandmouth level crossing has been rebuilt twice in living memory.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two helpers stack up in front of one third form. Has puts it in the perfect and been turns the crossing into the thing that was worked on.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Rebuild would leave the sentence with no time in it at all, and rebuilt on its own would claim the crossing did the rebuilding.

notice_set.sentence: The last two ferries out of Sandmouth have been cancelled.
notice_set.question: Can you sail from Sandmouth this evening?
notice_set.why: Have been cancelled is one unit. The helpers carry the time and cancelled names what was done, so the sailings are off.

notice_set.sentence: The footbridge is inspected every spring.
notice_set.question: Does the footbridge inspect anything?
notice_set.why: Inspected sits straight after is, and the third form after be always turns the sentence round: the bridge is what gets looked at.

notice_set.sentence: The tunnel had been shut for a fortnight before anyone told the drivers.
notice_set.question: Which came first, the shutting or the telling?
notice_set.why: Shut is the third form of shut and carries no time by itself. Had been in front of it is what sets the shutting earlier than the telling.

notice_set.sentence: The route has changed.
notice_set.question: Did somebody change it, or did it change on its own?
notice_set.why: There is no be in front of changed, so nobody has been put in the sentence. Have plus the third form only says the change reaches now.

notice_set.sentence: Three of the crossings have been rebuilt and two are still waiting.
notice_set.question: Is the work finished on those three?
notice_set.why: Rebuilt names a whole finished job, and the helpers hold it against now. The two still waiting sit outside that.

teach.rule_line: The third form needs a helper: have makes it perfect, be makes it passive.
teach.false_rule: That the third form is just the past tense with a different spelling. Written, driven, taken and shut are not past tenses; none of them can stand alone.

errors.wrong: The branch line has went out of service twice this month.
errors.right: The branch line has gone out of service twice this month.
errors.why_it_happens: Went is what the learner reaches for whenever the meaning is past, and everywhere else it works. After have, English wants the third form, and go is one of the verbs whose second and third forms look nothing like each other.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: went becomes gone.

errors.wrong: The window in the depot office was broke for most of the winter.
errors.right: The window in the depot office was broken for most of the winter.
errors.why_it_happens: Broke is a real word and a real past tense, so nothing feels missing when the learner writes it. After be the sentence needs the third form, and the -en ending is the only thing marking it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: broke becomes broken.

errors.wrong: By March the new platform had already build.
errors.right: By March the new platform had already been built.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has the helper and the idea of a finished job, but has dropped the be that makes the platform the thing worked on rather than the thing doing the work.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word and one ending: build becomes been built.

pays_in.note: Every stage of a process description is be plus this form.
pays_in.model: The treated water is then pumped into a holding tank on the ridge.

pays_in.note: Every perfect and every passive in an essay depends on this form.
pays_in.model: Rural bus routes have been cut faster than most councils expected.

pays_in.note: Passages carry long chains of helpers, and the chain is where the meaning sits.
pays_in.model: The scheme had been abandoned before the funding was formally withdrawn.

used_in.quote: Every stage of the heat pump diagram is written with be plus this form, and a wrong third form breaks every one of them.
The passage stacks helpers in front of one third form, and a question turns on reading the whole stack rather than the last word.

payload.sentence: The last two ferries have been cancelled.
payload.question: Are those ferries running?

feedback.why_key: Cancelled is the third form and it names what was done to the ferries. The helpers in front of it hold that against now.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the helper and the third form as one unit.

payload.sentence: The Norland marshes were flooded again last winter.
payload.question: Who or what did the flooding?

feedback.why_key: Flooded sits after were, so the marshes are what it happened to. Nobody has been named as the cause anywhere in the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: After be, ask what the subject had done to it.

payload.context: From a first draft about rural bus services.
payload.sentence: Passenger numbers on the branch line have fell every winter.
reasons: the verb after have is not the third form
the helper does not match the subject
the time named is already finished
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Fell is the second form. After have, fall wants fallen, and the two forms are not interchangeable however similar they sound.
feedback.feed_forward: After have, check you are on the third form, not the second.

payload.context: From a note on the works at Ashfield.
payload.stem: Four of the level crossings have been ___ (rebuild) since the works began.

feedback.why_key: Build is one of the verbs whose second and third forms are the same word, so built covers both jobs here.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn irregular verbs in threes, not in pairs.

payload.context: From a description of a recycling plant.
payload.stem: The waste is ___ (grind) into pellets before it is dried.

feedback.why_key: Grind, ground, ground. The third form here looks like an unrelated word, which is exactly why it has to be learned rather than worked out.
feedback.feed_forward: When the -ed ending sounds wrong, check the irregular list.

payload.context: Two neighbours on the stairs of a block of flats.
payload.stem: The lift has ___ (break) down three times this week.

feedback.why_key: Break, broke, broken. Broke is the second form and it cannot follow has, however natural it sounds out loud.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the three forms in order before you choose one.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a change in a town centre.

expected: the old market hall has been taken over by a supermarket

feedback.why_key: Two helpers then the third form, in that order, and only then the doer. Has been taken never comes apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the helpers together and put the third form straight after them.

payload.given: Somebody stole the copper from the hall roof. The hall has been shut ever since.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the first sentence so that the copper is what the sentence is about.

expected: was stolen from the hall roof
has been stolen from the hall roof

feedback.why_key: Steal, stole, stolen. Once be arrives, only the third form will do, and the thief drops out of the sentence entirely.
feedback.feed_forward: Put be in front, then reach for the third form.

payload.audio_text: The barriers have been left down again.

expected: the barriers have been left down again
the barriers've been left down again
the barriers been left down again

feedback.why_key: Have been runs together into almost nothing in speech. What survives is the third form, and on its own it tells you very little.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for two weak syllables in front of the main verb.

payload.sentence: Two of the surveyors have wrote to the council about the outfall pipe.

feedback.why_key: Write, wrote, written. Wrote can be a whole verb by itself, which is why it slips in after have where it cannot go.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the second form to the third after any helper.

payload.prompt_text: A building in your town has changed hands and is used for something else now. Write one sentence saying what has happened to it.

feedback.why_key: Saying what has happened to a building rather than who did it is exactly the job this form was built for.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the building first and the third form after the helper.

payload.prompt_text: Take the process diagram you described last week and rewrite two of its stages so that each one runs on be plus the third form. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: A process has no interesting doer, so every stage naturally lands on be plus the third form, and the diagram reads as one connected sequence.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the material first, then the helper, then the third form.

points.title: Looking back at an earlier event from a moment further on

point_json.grammar_name: The perfect: what the word means

teach.can_do: I can see the two times inside a perfect sentence and say which is which.
teach.why_it_matters: One idea covers the present perfect, the past perfect and the future perfect. Learn it once here and three later tenses cost you almost nothing.
teach.meaning: A perfect form always holds two moments at once. There is the moment something happened, and there is a second moment you are standing at, looking back at it. Have puts you at now. Had puts you at some point in the past. Will have puts you at a point ahead. The event is always earlier than the place you are standing, and the sentence is really about the standing place.

form.pattern: a helper + the third form: have / has + third form, had + third form, will have + third form
notes: Which helper you choose only says where you are standing: at now, at a past moment, or at a moment ahead
The third form itself never changes, whichever helper is in front of it
In speech the helper shrinks to 've, 's or 'd and can nearly disappear, which is why it has to be listened for on purpose
form.negative: Not attaches to the helper and never to the third form: has not arrived, had not arrived, will not have arrived.
form.question: The helper moves to the front: Has it arrived? Had it arrived? Will it have arrived?

marks.label: stand here and it is: had done
stand here and it is: has done
stand here and it is: will have done

spec.caption: The event never moves. What moves is the place you are looking back from.

worked_example.sentence: By the time the inspectors reached the plant, the crew had cleared the yard.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence stands at the moment the inspectors arrived and looks back from there. Had is what puts you at that earlier vantage point instead of at today.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Have cleared would drag the vantage point forward to now, and the state of the yard this morning would become the point of the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Halida has finished the water samples.
notice_set.question: Where is the speaker standing when they say this?
options: at the moment the samples were finished
notice_set.why: Has puts the vantage point at now. The finishing happened earlier; the sentence is about how things stand today.

notice_set.sentence: Halida had finished the water samples.
notice_set.question: Where is the speaker standing?
options: at some earlier moment, looking further back
notice_set.why: Had drops the vantage point into the past. Something else was going on at that moment, and the finishing was already behind it.

notice_set.sentence: By June the team will have finished the water samples.
notice_set.question: Is the finishing before or after June?
notice_set.why: Will have puts the vantage point at June and looks back from there, so the finishing has to be on the near side of it.

notice_set.sentence: The gates had been locked when the delivery arrived.
notice_set.question: Which came first?
notice_set.why: The vantage point is the delivery, and had puts the locking earlier than it. The order is stated, not guessed.

notice_set.sentence: The gates were locked when the delivery arrived.
notice_set.question: Which came first?
notice_set.why: With no perfect helper, nothing sets one before the other. The locking could have been going on at that moment or could have happened earlier.

teach.rule_line: A perfect form has two times: when it happened, and where you look back from.
teach.false_rule: That perfect means finished. It means earlier than the moment you are standing at, and plenty of perfect sentences describe things still going on.

errors.wrong: When we got to the depot, the fitters left already.
errors.right: When we got to the depot, the fitters had already left.
errors.why_it_happens: Both events are past, so both verbs come out in the past simple and the reader is trusted to work out the order. English marks the earlier one instead of leaving it to be guessed at.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: left becomes had left.

errors.wrong: By next spring the council will finish the repairs to the sea wall.
errors.right: By next spring the council will have finished the repairs to the sea wall.
errors.why_it_happens: By next spring names a vantage point ahead, but the whole situation is in the future, so the plain future arrives first. The looking-back part is what goes missing.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: will finish becomes will have finished.

errors.wrong: Since the plant was fitted with filters, the river ran clear.
errors.right: Since the plant was fitted with filters, the river has run clear.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner looks at the running and decides it is past, which it is. What never gets chosen is the vantage point, and the first half of the sentence has already fixed it at now.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: ran becomes has run.

pays_in.note: Any essay comparing now with earlier has to choose a vantage point on purpose.
pays_in.model: Since the levy was introduced, household waste has fallen in almost every district.

pays_in.note: A projection stands at a future year and looks back at it.
pays_in.model: By 2040 the share of electricity generated from wind will have roughly doubled.

pays_in.note: The order of events is carried by these helpers, not by the order of sentences.
pays_in.model: The site had been abandoned long before the survey team arrived.

used_in.quote: The passage tells its events out of order and relies on the helper in front of each verb to put them back in order.
The final year on the chart is a vantage point, and the strongest sentence in the answer stands there and looks back.

payload.sentence: By the time Feras rang, the office had shut.
payload.question: Which came first?

feedback.why_key: The ringing is the vantage point and had puts the shutting on the far side of it. That is the whole job of the helper.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the vantage point first, then place the other event.

payload.sentence: By 2040 the reservoir will have lost a third of its capacity.
payload.question: Where does the losing sit?

feedback.why_key: Will have stands you at 2040 and looks back, so the losing has to be finished by the time you get there.
feedback.feed_forward: Read by plus a year as a place to stand, not as a date.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about river quality.
payload.sentence: Since the outfall was capped, the water quality improved every year.
reasons: the stretch of time opened at the start is still running
the improving has not begun yet
the third form of the verb is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The first half puts the vantage point at now and the second half quietly moves it back into the past. The reader has to pick one.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the vantage point once, then keep the verbs on it.

payload.context: From a note on a long-running field study.
payload.stem: By the time the funding ran out, the team ___ (record) eleven full seasons.

feedback.why_key: The funding running out is the vantage point, and the eleven seasons are all behind it, so the helper has to be had.
feedback.feed_forward: Put had in front when the other verb is already past.

payload.context: From a projection for the Verdon catchment.
payload.stem: By 2040 demand ___ (rise) by almost a fifth.

feedback.why_key: By 2040 is a place to stand, not a date for the rising. Standing there and looking back needs all three words.
feedback.feed_forward: Say will have, then the third form.

payload.context: A colleague catching up with someone after a fortnight away.
payload.stem: The rota ___ (change) twice while you were off.

feedback.why_key: The point of saying it is what the listener is walking back into today, so the vantage point is now.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who the news is for before you pick the helper.

payload.given: The council approved the plan in March. The developer pulled out in February.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that makes the order plain, standing at the moment of the approval.
payload.starter: By the time the council approved the plan, ___

expected: the developer had already pulled out

feedback.why_key: The approval is where you are standing, so the pulling out has to be marked as earlier or the reader will read them in the order given.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the earlier event with had, every time.

payload.audio_text: They'd already signed it off by then.

expected: they'd already signed it off by then
they had already signed it off by then
theyd already signed it off by then

feedback.why_key: The 'd is a single consonant and it is the only thing setting the signing earlier than by then. Miss it and the order is gone.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a d riding on the end of the subject.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different reports on the same depot.
sentences: When the auditors arrived, the depot had closed.
When the auditors arrived, the depot closed.
meanings: They found the gates already locked; the closing was over before they got there.
Their arrival and the closing came one after the other on the same day.

feedback.why_key: One helper is the difference between finding a closed depot and watching it close. Nothing else in the two sentences has moved.
feedback.feed_forward: Read had as a signal that you have jumped backwards.

payload.sentence: Since the plant was fitted with filters, the river ran clear all summer.

feedback.why_key: The opening clause fixes the vantage point at now, and the second half has to stand there too or the sentence contradicts itself.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the vantage point at the start and keep it.

payload.prompt_text: Something in your town was already finished before most people noticed it. Write one sentence that stands at the moment people noticed and looks back.

feedback.why_key: The sentence has to hold two moments, and the reader can only see which is which because you marked the earlier one.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the vantage point first, then the earlier event.

payload.prompt_text: Go back to the projection chart you described and add one sentence that stands at the final year on it and looks back at what has happened by then. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A chart that ends in a future year invites exactly this sentence, and it is the one an examiner reads as an overview rather than a list.
feedback.feed_forward: Stand at the last year on the chart and look back.

points.title: Saying that something from before still counts right now

teach.can_do: I can say that something from earlier still counts at this moment.
teach.why_it_matters: The commonest answers in Part 1 are this form: what you have done, what has changed, and how long you have been at it.
teach.meaning: This form takes an earlier event and hands it to now. It does that in three ways. It can put something on your record, so an experience from any point in your life counts today. It can report a past event whose result is still in front of you. And it can measure a stretch that started earlier and has not stopped. In all three, now is what the sentence is really about.

notes: has with he, she, it and any singular noun; have with I, you, we, they and any plural
've and 's in speech and in a friendly message; the full words in an essay
The third form never changes for the subject. All of that work happens in the helper
form.negative: have not / haven't + third form; has not / hasn't + third form
form.question: Have you + third form ...? Has the council + third form ...?

spec.caption: The arrow is the whole point. Take it away and all you have is an ordinary past sentence.

worked_example.sentence: Yusra has run the night shift at the Marlow depot three times.
worked_example.why_this_form: The three occasions are on her record now, and that record is what the sentence is offering. When each one happened is not being claimed at all.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Ran would drop the three occasions inside some particular stretch of the past, and a listener would immediately want to know which stretch.

notice_set.sentence: Kester has worked on three of the coastal reserves.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you when he did that?
notice_set.why: The form deliberately leaves the when out. What it puts on the table is that the experience is his, today.

notice_set.sentence: Somebody has taken the site keys.
notice_set.question: Are the keys where they should be?
notice_set.why: The taking is over and done. What the sentence is really reporting is the hole it left, which is still there.

notice_set.sentence: Nuala has lived on the Ashfield road all her life.
notice_set.question: Does she live there now?
notice_set.why: The stretch runs from her birth up to this moment without stopping, and she is standing at the end of it.

notice_set.sentence: The tide has turned.
notice_set.question: Is the water doing now what it was doing an hour ago?
notice_set.why: The turning is a finished event, and the reason for mentioning it is that the water is going the other way at this moment.

notice_set.sentence: Have you eaten?
notice_set.question: What does the person asking want to know?
notice_set.why: The question is not really about the meal. It is about the state you are in as they ask it.

teach.rule_line: Use it when an earlier event is still doing work at this moment.
teach.false_rule: That it is just the past tense built with have. The past tense reports; this form makes a claim about now, and that claim can be wrong.

errors.wrong: The number of complaints have risen sharply this term.
errors.right: The number of complaints has risen sharply this term.
errors.why_it_happens: Complaints is plural and it is sitting right next to the helper, so the ear picks it up. The real subject is the number, which is singular and three words further back.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: So far this year the clinic saw four hundred more patients than last year.
errors.right: So far this year the clinic has seen four hundred more patients than last year.
errors.why_it_happens: So far this year is a stretch the speaker is still inside, but the seeing feels like a finished set of events, so the past simple arrives first and the stretch is quietly abandoned.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: saw becomes has seen.

errors.wrong: The committee have chose a new site for the depot.
errors.right: The committee have chosen a new site for the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: Chose is a whole verb on its own and it means the right thing, so nothing sounds missing. Choose is one of the many verbs whose second and third forms differ by a single ending.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: chose becomes chosen.

pays_in.note: Nearly every answer about your life or your job opens with this form.
pays_in.model: I've worked at the same clinic since I finished my training.

pays_in.note: It is how an essay says that a change has already landed.
pays_in.model: Councils have cut rural bus routes in almost every part of the country.

pays_in.note: The helper is unstressed, so the whole claim about now rides on one weak syllable.
pays_in.model: They've moved the meeting to Thursday.

used_in.quote: How long have you been doing that, and has it changed much? Both follow-ups are answered in this form or not at all.
The essay has to establish that working lives have already changed before it can argue about why.

payload.sentence: The clinic has taken on two more nurses.
payload.question: Are those nurses there now?

feedback.why_key: The hiring is finished, and the reason for mentioning it is the staffing today. That is what the helper is carrying.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what the sentence claims about this moment.

payload.sentence: Somebody has left the yard gate open.
payload.question: Is the gate open at this moment?

feedback.why_key: Nobody says this to report an action. They say it because of the state the action left behind, and that state is now.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the result the speaker can still see.

payload.context: From a first draft about clinic waiting times.
payload.sentence: The number of patients waiting more than a month have risen again.
reasons: the helper does not match the real subject
the third form of the verb is wrong
the time named is already finished
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The thing that has risen is the number, and a number is one thing however many patients are inside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the head noun, then choose has or have.

payload.context: From a paragraph on rural health services.
payload.stem: Three of the village surgeries ___ (close) since the trust was reorganised.

feedback.why_key: The reorganisation opened a stretch that nobody has shut, so the closures are counted up to this moment.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether the stretch has an end before choosing.

payload.context: Two colleagues on a Monday morning.
payload.stem: The committee ___ (choose) a new site for the depot.

feedback.why_key: Choose, chose, chosen. Only the third form follows the helper, and a committee can take either has or have in British English.
feedback.feed_forward: Run the three forms before you write the third one.

payload.context: From an essay on what school leavers do next.
payload.stem: The share of school leavers going straight into work ___ (fall) sharply.

feedback.why_key: Leavers is plural and close by, but the thing that has fallen is the share, and a share is singular.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the middle of the subject and read it again.

payload.given: The council shut two libraries. Both buildings are still standing empty.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that ties the shutting to how things stand today.

expected: has shut two libraries and both buildings are still standing empty
has shut two libraries, and both buildings are still standing empty
has shut two libraries and both are still standing empty

feedback.why_key: The empty buildings are the reason anyone is mentioning the closures, so the closures have to reach forward to them.
feedback.feed_forward: When the result is the point, use the helper.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a bus service.

expected: the timetable has been rewritten twice this term

feedback.why_key: This term is a stretch still running, and the two rewrites are counted inside it up to today.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep has been together and put the third form next.

payload.audio_text: They've moved the meeting to Thursday.

expected: they've moved the meeting to thursday
they have moved the meeting to thursday
theyve moved the meeting to thursday

feedback.why_key: They've and they both take one syllable in ordinary speech. The whole claim about where the meeting is now hangs on that v.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a v at the end of the subject.

payload.sentence: So far this year the clinic saw four hundred more patients than last year.

feedback.why_key: So far this year says the counting is still going on. A finished form there tells the reader the year is over.
feedback.feed_forward: If the counting continues, use the helper.

payload.context: Ruben is telling a colleague how the summer is going at the depot.
payload.sentence: They have took on two extra drivers for the season.
reasons: the verb after the helper is not the third form
the helper does not match the subject
the season is already over
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Take, took, taken. Took can be a whole verb by itself, which is exactly why it slips in where only taken belongs.
feedback.feed_forward: After have, use the form that cannot stand alone.

payload.prompt_text: Something about your job or your course is not the way it was when you started. Say one sentence about what is different now.

feedback.why_key: A change that has landed is exactly what this form is for, and it is what an examiner hears as an answer rather than a fact.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what is different now, not what happened in March.

payload.prompt_text: Answer the Part 1 question about your work or study in two sentences. Make the first one a change that has already landed. Forty-five seconds.

feedback.why_key: Opening on a change rather than a fact gives the examiner something to follow up, and it puts the form where it is heard first.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with what has changed, then add the detail.

points.title: Saying how long something has gone on, or when it started

point_json.grammar_name: for and since with the present perfect

teach.can_do: I can say how long something has been going on, or when it began, and choose the right word for each.
teach.why_it_matters: How long have you...? is one of the commonest questions you will be asked, and a great many answers to it begin with the wrong word.
teach.meaning: Both words hang a stretch of time on a sentence that reaches up to now, and they hang it by different ends. For takes the length: how much time has gone by. Since takes the front edge: the moment the clock started running. That is why a whole clause about an event can follow since and cannot follow for. Choose by asking what your own words actually measure.

form.pattern: have / has + third form + for + a length, or + since + a starting point
notes: for + a length: for ten minutes, for three years, for ages, for as long as I can remember
since + a point: since Tuesday, since 2019, since the flood, since my first term
since + a whole clause with a past simple verb inside it: since I left school
How long...? is the question that both of them answer
form.negative: haven't + third form + for is the ordinary way to name a gap: I haven't seen her for months.
form.question: How long have you + third form ...?

spec.caption: Since names the left-hand end of the line. For measures the line itself.

worked_example.sentence: Devi has rented the same flat since she finished her degree.
worked_example.why_this_form: Finishing a degree is a moment you could mark on a calendar, so it names the front edge of the stretch rather than measuring how much of it there has been.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: For needs a length after it, and a degree is not a length, so the reader would stall trying to work out how long one is supposed to be.

notice_set.sentence: The road has been closed for three days.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence name the day it closed?
notice_set.why: Three days measures the gap. You could work the day out yourself, but the sentence has not told you.

notice_set.sentence: The road has been closed since Tuesday.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence name the day it closed?
notice_set.why: Since points straight at the front edge, so the day is stated and the length is left for you to count.

notice_set.sentence: Idris has been in the job for six months.
notice_set.question: Is he still in it?
notice_set.why: With this helper the six months run right up to the moment of speaking, and he is standing at the end of them.

notice_set.sentence: We haven't had a proper bus service for years.
notice_set.question: Is there a proper bus service now?
notice_set.why: The stretch being measured is a gap, and the gap reaches this morning.

notice_set.sentence: Since the mill shut, the village has lost both its shops.
notice_set.question: Did the shops go before or after the mill?
notice_set.why: Since sets the mill closing as the front edge, and everything the sentence reports happens inside the stretch after it.

teach.rule_line: For measures the length of the stretch; since names the moment it started.
teach.false_rule: That for goes with numbers and since goes with dates. For ages has no number in it, and since I was small has no date in it.

contrast.question: Am I naming how long it lasted, or the moment it began?

fork.answer: How long: a fortnight, six years, ages, as long as I can remember
When it began: Tuesday, 2019, the flood, I left school

a.text: The corner shop has been shut for the summer.
a.means: Someone shut it on purpose for that whole stretch, and it opens again when the stretch runs out.

b.text: The corner shop has been shut since the summer.
b.means: It shut at some point in the summer and it is still shut today, with no end announced.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote since a fortnight. That hands your reader a fortnight as though it were a date, and they stall working out which day you mean. A fortnight is a length, and lengths take for.

edge_case.text: Since also means because, and a since clause of that kind has nothing to do with time at all. And in ordinary speech for often just disappears: I've lived here three years is perfectly normal. Since never disappears.

contrast.stronger_test: Try putting a period of in front of your words. If it fits, they measure a length and take for. If instead you could write them in a diary, they take since.

worked_pairs.a: The lift has been out of order for a fortnight.
worked_pairs.b: The lift has been out of order since the flood.
worked_pairs.gloss: A fortnight measures how much trouble there has been. The flood names the moment the trouble started.

worked_pairs.a: Zeynep has taught here for nine years.
worked_pairs.b: Zeynep has taught here since the college moved.
worked_pairs.gloss: One counts the years; the other picks the event they started from and leaves the counting to you.

worked_pairs.a: We have had the same landlord for as long as I can remember.
worked_pairs.b: We have had the same landlord since we signed the first lease.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: as long as I can remember
worked_pairs.gloss: Neither one has a number in it, and the choice is still obvious once you ask what the words are doing.

errors.wrong: The boiler has been broken since three weeks.
errors.right: The boiler has been broken for three weeks.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages cover both jobs with one word, so the learner picks whichever English word they met first and uses it everywhere. Nothing in the sentence itself signals that a length and a starting point need different words.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: since becomes for.
errors.l1_note: Several languages use a single preposition for both jobs.

errors.wrong: Devi has rented the flat for she started the course.
errors.right: Devi has rented the flat since she started the course.
errors.why_it_happens: A clause after for feels natural because for can introduce a reason. Here the clause is naming a moment rather than giving a reason, and only since opens a time clause of that kind.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: for becomes since.

errors.wrong: Since the new landlord took over, the rent went up twice.
errors.right: Since the new landlord took over, the rent has gone up twice.
errors.why_it_happens: Since opens a stretch that reaches to now, but each rise feels like a finished event, so the past simple comes out. By the time the second verb is written, the word that opened the stretch is a whole clause away.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: went becomes has gone.

pays_in.note: How long have you lived there is asked in nearly every Part 1.
pays_in.model: I've been in the same flat for about four years now.

pays_in.note: Chart answers measure spans and name starting points constantly.
pays_in.model: Household water use has fallen steadily since the meters were fitted.

pays_in.note: In a form-filling task the answer changes with which of the two words arrives.
pays_in.model: She's been a member since March.

used_in.quote: The follow-up on this card is always how long, and the answer is one of these two words plus a stretch.
A membership date and a membership length are two different answers, and the word in front tells you which one you are hearing.

payload.sentence: The lift has been out of order since the flood.
payload.question: Does the sentence tell you when it broke?

feedback.why_key: The flood is the moment the trouble started, and since is the word that points at a moment rather than measuring one.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the words name a moment or a length.

payload.sentence: The lift has been out of order for a fortnight.
payload.question: Does the sentence tell you which day it broke?

feedback.why_key: A fortnight measures the gap. You could count backwards yourself, but the sentence has not named a day.
feedback.feed_forward: A length tells you how much, never which day.

payload.context: Bea is complaining to a neighbour about the heating.
payload.sentence: The boiler has been broken since three weeks.
reasons: the words after it measure a length rather than naming a moment
the helper is the wrong one
the third form of the verb is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Three weeks is an amount of time, not a place on the calendar, so the word in front of it has to be the measuring one.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the words after the blank before you choose.

payload.context: From a letter to a landlord about repairs.
payload.stem: The kitchen tap has dripped ___ the middle of January.

feedback.why_key: The middle of January is a place on the calendar, so it can only be the front edge of the stretch.
feedback.feed_forward: If you could circle it on a calendar, use since.

payload.context: Two people talking at a bus stop.
payload.stem: I've worked at the sorting office ___ nearly eleven years.

feedback.why_key: Eleven years is an amount, and amounts are measured rather than pointed at.
feedback.feed_forward: If it answers how much, use for.

payload.given: Devi moved into the flat in 2019. She is still living there.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that names the moment the stretch began rather than measuring it.

expected: has lived in the flat since 2019
has been in the flat since 2019

feedback.why_key: A year is a point you can put your finger on, so it goes after the pointing word and the counting is left to the reader.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the year, then reach for since.

payload.audio_text: We've had the same landlord since we moved in.

expected: we've had the same landlord since we moved in
we have had the same landlord since we moved in
weve had the same landlord since we moved in

feedback.why_key: The 've is almost nothing and the choosing word is unstressed too, so both of the parts that carry the meaning are the quiet ones.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the small words between the subject and the verb.

items.decision_cue: they are due back in September

payload.context: The bakery closes every year while the owners are away, and they are due back in September.
payload.stem: The bakery has been shut ___ the summer.

options.why_this_means: That the summer is the whole planned length of the closure, and it ends when the summer does.
That the summer is when the closure started, and nothing has been said about it ending.

feedback.why_key: A closure with a known end is a measured stretch, and the summer is being used as the measurement rather than as a starting point.
feedback.feed_forward: If the end is already known, measure the stretch.

items.decision_cue: nobody knows when it will open

payload.context: The bakery closed when the owners fell ill and nobody knows when it will open.
payload.stem: The bakery has been shut ___ the summer.

options.why_this_means: That the summer is the whole planned length of the closure, and it ends when the summer does.
That the summer is when the closure started, and nothing has been said about it ending.

feedback.why_key: With no end in view there is nothing to measure, so the summer can only be the moment the shutters came down.
feedback.feed_forward: With no end in sight, name the beginning.

items.decision_cue: it reopens in April as it does every year

payload.context: The pool shuts while the boilers are serviced, and it reopens in April as it does every year.
payload.stem: The pool has been closed ___ the winter.

options.why_this_means: That the winter is the agreed length of the closure and swimming starts again at the end of it.
That the closure began in the winter and is still running with no end fixed.

feedback.why_key: A yearly shutdown with a reopening date is a length of time, and the winter is being used to state that length.
feedback.feed_forward: A planned closure is measured, not dated.

items.decision_cue: the repairs have still not been funded

payload.context: A pipe burst under the changing rooms and the repairs have still not been funded.
payload.stem: The pool has been closed ___ the winter.

options.why_this_means: That the winter is the agreed length of the closure and swimming starts again at the end of it.
That the closure began in the winter and is still running with no end fixed.

feedback.why_key: Nobody has agreed a length here, so the winter can only be the point where the trouble started.
feedback.feed_forward: Unfixed endings take the pointing word.

items.decision_cue: the flat he is living in at the moment

payload.context: Marek is telling a friend about the flat he is living in at the moment.
payload.stem: I've had the place ___ the winter.

options.why_this_means: That he took it on a winter let and it runs out when the winter does.
That he moved in some time during the winter and is still there with no end date.

follow_up.question: Which one says he will have to move out at the end of the winter?

feedback.why_key: Both sentences are ordinary English about a real flat. One of them has a moving-out date built into it and the other does not.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether the end is already fixed, then choose.

payload.context: Two versions of the same note taped inside a shop window.
sentences: The corner shop has been shut for the summer.
The corner shop has been shut since the summer.
meanings: It was shut on purpose for that whole stretch and it opens again at the end of it.
It shut at some point during the summer and it is still shut, with no reopening announced.

feedback.why_key: One word tells a customer to come back in September and the other tells them not to hold their breath. Nothing else in the note has changed.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the word in front of the time, not the time.

payload.context: From a message to a letting agent.
payload.sentence: The extractor fan has not worked since more than a month.
reasons: the words after it measure a length rather than naming a moment
the negative is in the wrong place
the helper does not match the subject
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: More than a month is an amount, and amounts cannot be pointed at. The sentence needs the measuring word instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Test the words: are they an amount or a date?

payload.prompt_text: Think about where you live now. Say one sentence about how long you have been there and one about when you arrived.

feedback.why_key: The same stretch of your life described from both ends is the cleanest possible demonstration that the two words are not interchangeable.
feedback.feed_forward: Measure the stretch once, then name its start.

payload.prompt_text: Answer the Part 1 question about your home in three sentences. One must measure a stretch and one must name where the stretch began. Forty-five seconds.

feedback.why_key: A Part 1 answer that gives both the length and the starting point sounds like a person talking rather than a person answering a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the length first, then the starting point.

points.title: Saying whether something is early, late, overdue or just done

point_json.grammar_name: already, yet, just, still, ever, never, so far, recently

teach.can_do: I can drop already, yet, just and still into the slot English keeps for each of them.
teach.why_it_matters: These words are cheap to learn and they carry a lot: whether something is early, late, expected or overdue. A misplaced one is heard immediately.
teach.meaning: These small words do not change what happened. They tell your listener how it sits against what was expected. Already says it happened sooner than anyone thought. Yet says the thing is still owed and somebody is waiting. Just says it happened a moment ago. Still, in a negative, says the waiting has gone on longer than it should. Ever and never open and shut a whole lifetime of chances.

form.pattern: have / has + already, just, never, ever + third form, and yet at the end of the sentence
notes: already, just, never and ever sit between the helper and the third form: I have already sent it
yet goes at the end and belongs to questions and negatives: Have you sent it yet? I haven't sent it yet
still comes in front of the helper in a negative: I still haven't sent it, and that order is what makes it sound impatient
so far and recently can go at the front or at the end: So far we have had no reply, or We have had no reply so far
form.negative: haven't + third form + yet is the plain negative; still haven't + third form is the impatient one.
form.question: Have you ever + third form ...? Have you + third form ... yet?

left.role: the slot between the helper and the verb
left.text: has already gone / has never gone / has just gone

right.role: the slot at the end of the sentence
right.text: hasn't gone yet / hasn't gone so far

spec.caption: Two slots, and each of these words has learned which one belongs to it. Swapping them is what gets noticed.

worked_example.sentence: The council has already published the figures, and nobody has commented on them yet.
worked_example.why_this_form: Already sits inside the verb and says the publishing beat expectations. Yet sits at the end and says the comments are still owed.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Put yet in the middle and the sentence stops sounding like English. Put already at the end and the timing turns into an afterthought.

notice_set.sentence: The results have already gone out.
notice_set.question: Did they go out sooner than people expected?
notice_set.why: That is the whole job of the word. Without it the sentence would just report the sending.

notice_set.sentence: The results haven't gone out yet.
notice_set.question: Is somebody waiting for them?
notice_set.why: Yet marks a thing as owed. Nobody uses it about something no one is waiting for.

notice_set.sentence: They still haven't answered my letter.
notice_set.question: How does the writer feel?
options: they are fed up with waiting
they are surprised it came so fast
notice_set.why: Putting still in front of the helper is what carries the impatience. Move it and the complaint disappears.

notice_set.sentence: I've just seen the notice.
notice_set.question: When did the speaker see it?
notice_set.why: Just narrows the moment right down to the recent past, which is why it sits tight against the verb.

notice_set.sentence: Have you ever worked a night shift?
notice_set.question: What stretch of time does the question cover?
options: your whole life up to now
notice_set.why: Ever throws the question open across every chance the person has had, which is why the answer is a record rather than a date.

teach.rule_line: already, just, never and ever go inside the verb; yet goes at the end.
teach.false_rule: That these words switch the present perfect on. They live happily in other tenses too: the meeting had already started; I still work there; she never wrote back.

errors.wrong: I have sent already the invoice to the office.
errors.right: I have already sent the invoice to the office.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner puts the small word after the whole verb because that is where it goes in many other languages. English keeps a slot open between the helper and the third form and expects it to be filled from there.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: already goes in front of sent.
errors.l1_note: Several languages place these adverbs after the verb phrase.

errors.wrong: Have you yet finished the handover notes?
errors.right: Have you finished the handover notes yet?
errors.why_it_happens: Yet has been treated like already and dropped into the middle slot. In an everyday question it belongs at the end, where it hands the whole sentence its sense of waiting.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: yet goes to the end.

errors.wrong: I have already sent the invoice last Friday.
errors.right: I sent the invoice last Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: Already has been stored as a trigger for this form, so it fires and drags the helper in with it. The named finished day is not part of that stored rule, so nothing arrives to stop it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: have.

pays_in.note: These words carry the timing of an answer at almost no cost.
pays_in.model: I've just started a new course, so my week looks completely different.

pays_in.note: A letter saying what is done and what is owed runs on them.
pays_in.model: I have already sent two reminders and have had no reply so far.

pays_in.note: Whether a thing is finished or still owed can turn on one unstressed word.
pays_in.model: They haven't confirmed it yet.

used_in.quote: Chasing a refund is entirely a matter of naming what you have already done and what has still not happened.
A routine answer becomes interesting the moment it says what has just changed rather than what happens every day.

payload.sentence: They still haven't printed a correction.
payload.question: How does the speaker feel about the wait?
options: it has gone on too long

feedback.why_key: Still in front of the helper is a complaint. The same sentence without it is only a report.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the position of the small word as a tone of voice.

payload.sentence: Two of the three reports have already been signed off.
payload.question: Is the third one signed off?

feedback.why_key: Counting two out of three only makes sense while the job is running, and already says the counting is further on than expected.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a running total as a job still open.

payload.context: From a message to a supplier.
payload.sentence: We have sent already two reminders about the invoice.
reasons: the small word is in the wrong slot
the helper is the wrong one
the third form of the verb is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The slot between the helper and the third form is the one already lives in. Pushed out past the verb it sounds translated.
feedback.feed_forward: Put already straight after have or has.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a local newspaper, and nobody expected the apology so soon.
payload.stem: The paper has ___ apologised, which took everyone by surprise.

feedback.why_key: The surprise is that it happened sooner than anyone thought, and that is precisely what this word contributes.
feedback.feed_forward: Use already when the timing beats expectation.

payload.context: One colleague chasing another about an application.
payload.stem: Have you heard back from the agency ___?

feedback.why_key: A question about something owed ends on this word, and putting it anywhere else in the question breaks it.
feedback.feed_forward: End a question about something owed with yet.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a complaint sent to a newspaper.

expected: the editor has still not answered any of the letters

feedback.why_key: Still goes in front of the negative, and that order is what turns a report into a complaint.
feedback.feed_forward: Say still before not, not after it.

payload.given: We sent the deposit form in March. The agency has not replied.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so it says the reply is overdue and you have run out of patience.

feedback.why_key: One word moved to the front of the negative is the whole difference between reporting silence and objecting to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Front the still when you want it to sting.

expected: they have not confirmed it yet

feedback.why_key: Both of the words that carry the meaning here are unstressed, and the one at the end is the easiest of all to lose.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen right to the end of the sentence.

payload.sentence: They have already printed the correction last Thursday, which is more than I expected.

feedback.why_key: Last Thursday shuts the day, and no amount of already will let this helper stand next to a shut, named day.
feedback.feed_forward: When a day is named and over, drop the helper.

payload.context: Ruben is asking a colleague about a piece of work at the end of the day.
payload.sentence: Have you yet finished the handover notes?
reasons: that small word belongs at the end of the question
the helper is the wrong one
the third form of the verb is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Yet is not one of the words that live inside the verb. In an ordinary spoken question it waits at the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the question, then add yet.

payload.prompt_text: You are chasing something you were promised. Write one sentence saying what you have already done and one saying what has not happened.

feedback.why_key: Naming what is done and what is owed in that order is what makes a complaint sound reasonable rather than cross.
feedback.feed_forward: Put already inside the verb and yet at the end.

payload.prompt_text: Rewrite the opening paragraph of your last formal letter so that it names one thing already done and one thing still owed. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: An opening paragraph built on those two facts tells the reader exactly where the matter stands before any request is made.
feedback.feed_forward: State what is done, then state what is missing.

points.title: Saying whether somebody went and came back, or is still there

point_json.grammar_name: has been to and has gone to

teach.can_do: I can say whether someone went somewhere and came back, or is there at this moment.
teach.why_it_matters: One syllable decides whether your listener expects to see the person this afternoon. It is a small point and it goes wrong constantly.
teach.meaning: Both sentences describe a journey that has already started, and they disagree about where the traveller is standing while you read them. Been says the journey is finished in both directions: they went, they came back, and the trip is now part of what they have done. Gone says the journey is only half over: they set off and they have not returned, which is usually the reason they are being mentioned at all.

form.pattern: have / has been to + a place, or have / has gone to + a place
notes: been to takes to when you mean the trip: I have been to Marlow, not I have been in Marlow
you can count trips that are over, so been to takes twice, three times, several times; gone to cannot
been is also the plain third form of be, so it turns up in sentences with no travel in them at all
form.negative: haven't been to is the everyday negative; hasn't gone to usually means they never set off.
form.question: Have you ever been to ...? Where has she gone?

left.role: been to: the journey is finished both ways
left.text: Halida has been to the site office.

right.role: gone to: the journey is only half done
right.text: Halida has gone to the site office.

spec.caption: The difference is not where they went. It is where they are standing while you read the sentence.

worked_example.sentence: Two of the surveyors have been to the Norland reserve, so they know the access track.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence needs them back at the table, because it is using what they learned out there. Only the completed round trip leaves them in the room.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Gone would put both surveyors out at the reserve right now, and the second half of the sentence would have nobody left to know anything.

notice_set.sentence: Marek has gone to the harbour office.
notice_set.question: Can you speak to him where you are?
notice_set.why: The half-finished journey leaves him at the other end of it, which is why somebody said this to you in the first place.

notice_set.sentence: Marek has been to the harbour office.
notice_set.question: Can you speak to him where you are?
notice_set.why: The round trip is complete, so the office visit is behind him and he is back where you are.

notice_set.sentence: Have you ever been to a night market?
notice_set.question: What is the question about?
options: whether it has ever happened in your life
notice_set.why: Ever throws the question across a whole life, and only the completed round trip can be counted that way.

notice_set.sentence: Half the crew has gone to the yard.
notice_set.question: What is the office like at this moment?
notice_set.why: Half of them are at the other end of an unfinished journey, so the room they left is emptier than normal.

notice_set.sentence: It has been cold since the weekend.
notice_set.question: Is this sentence about a journey?
notice_set.why: Been here is just the plain third form of be. The travelling meaning only appears when to and a place follow it.

teach.rule_line: Been means they went and came back; gone means they are still at the other end.
teach.false_rule: That been and gone are two spellings of one idea. They put the traveller in two different places, and only one of them is in the room with you.

contrast.question: Is the person back, or are they still at the other end?

fork.answer: Back, and the trip is now part of what they have done
Still there, and that is exactly why they are not in front of you

a.text: Halida has been to the site office.
a.means: She went and she is back. You could turn round and ask her about it.

b.text: Halida has gone to the site office.
b.means: She is at the site office now, which is why you cannot find her.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote has gone. Your listener now expects an empty chair and starts planning round it. If she is sitting two desks away, been is the word that says so, and the whole difference is one syllable.

edge_case.text: Been is also the plain third form of be, so it appears in sentences with no travelling in them: it has been cold all week. And in speech been to happily takes a place that is really an appointment: I've been to the dentist.

contrast.stronger_test: Try adding and she's back now on the end. If the sentence takes it without complaint, been was the word you wanted. Gone refuses it outright.

worked_pairs.a: Kester has been to the Verdon gorge twice.
worked_pairs.b: Kester has gone to the Verdon gorge for the weekend.
worked_pairs.gloss: You can count trips that are over. A trip somebody is still on has no count yet, only a length.

worked_pairs.a: Half the team has been to the new depot and they say it is enormous.
worked_pairs.b: Half the team has gone to the new depot, so the office is quiet.
worked_pairs.gloss: The report needs them back in the room. The quiet office needs them out of it.

worked_pairs.a: I have been to Sandmouth, so I know the coast road.
worked_pairs.b: She has gone to Sandmouth, so she will not be in until Thursday.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so I know the coast road
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so she will not be in until Thursday
worked_pairs.gloss: One sentence uses the journey as knowledge. The other uses it as an absence.

errors.wrong: Nuala isn't at her desk. She has been to the wholesaler.
errors.right: Nuala isn't at her desk. She has gone to the wholesaler.
errors.why_it_happens: Been is the word learners meet first, in the question about experience, so it becomes the default for anything involving travel. Nothing in the sentence corrects it, and the result is a clear sentence saying the wrong thing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: been becomes gone.

errors.wrong: I went to Sandmouth three times, so I know the coast road well.
errors.right: I have been to Sandmouth three times, so I know the coast road well.
errors.why_it_happens: The three trips are over, so the past simple looks right. The point of the sentence is what the speaker knows today, and a finished form leaves that connection hanging.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: went becomes have been.

points.title: Saying whether the stretch of time you mean is over or still running

teach.can_do: I can tell somebody whether the stretch of time I mean is over or still running.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the choice English makes most often and learners get wrong most often. Both forms are already in your hands; only the decision is missing.
teach.meaning: Two sentences can describe exactly the same event and still disagree. What they disagree about is the stretch of time behind them. If that stretch has an end and the end has passed, the past simple reports the event and stops there. If the stretch has no end yet, the present perfect keeps the event attached to this moment and lets it go on counting. So the question is never what happened, but which stretch you are standing in.

form.pattern: present perfect: have / has + third form. past simple: the second form, or did + the plain form in questions and negatives
notes: The present perfect refuses a named, finished time. Put one beside it and the sentence breaks
The past simple is happy with a named time and just as happy without one
Both take for plus a length. For nine years sits comfortably in either, and on its own it decides nothing
form.negative: haven't + third form for the stretch still running; didn't + plain form for the stretch that is over.
form.question: Have you + third form ...? for the open stretch; Did you + plain form ...? for the closed one.

marks.label: a stretch with both ends fixed
a stretch with no end yet

spec.caption: Nothing about the event changes between the two lines. What changes is which stretch of time the speaker has in mind.

worked_example.sentence: Ashfield Rovers have played nine home games without losing one.
worked_example.why_this_form: The run is still going, and nine is a count up to this afternoon. A count up to this afternoon only makes sense while there are matches left.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Played on its own would say the run is over, nine is the final figure, and the tenth game went the other way.

notice_set.question: Is she there this term?

discovery.prompt: The sentences on the left and on the right describe the same kinds of events. Work out what is different about the situations behind them.
pairs: Zeynep has taught at the college for nine years.
Zeynep taught at the college for nine years.

candidate_rules.text: On the left, the stretch of time behind the sentence has no end yet.
On the left, the events happened more recently.
On the left, the sentence contains a word like for, since or yet.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether the stretch of time you mean has an end that has already passed.
teach.false_rule: That a handful of time words decide it for you. They do not. The situation decides, and any of those words can turn up on either side of the choice.

contrast.question: Is the stretch of time I mean over?

fork.answer: Over, and usually named: that term, in 2016, on my last shift, when I was training
Still running, or never named at all: this term, in my life, up to today

a.text: Zeynep taught at the Brackenfield college for nine years.
a.means: The nine years are closed. She teaches somewhere else now, or nowhere.

b.text: Zeynep has taught at the Brackenfield college for nine years.
b.means: The nine years are still running. She is in the staffroom this term.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose taught. To a reader that is a clean, clear sentence saying she has left the college. She has not. Nothing looks broken, which is exactly why this pair is expensive.

edge_case.text: Speakers of American English frequently take the past simple where a British speaker leaves the stretch open, and both are right in their own variety. Everything here is British-standard. Notice the difference once, then stop carrying it around.

contrast.stronger_test: Pin a dead date on the end of your sentence: on 3 March, in 2016. The past simple takes it without blinking. The present perfect throws it straight off, and that is your answer.

worked_pairs.a: Applications to the college have risen, so the timetable is being redrawn.
worked_pairs.b: Applications to the college rose sharply between 2009 and 2014.

points.title: Talking about an activity that has been running up to now and still shows

teach.can_do: I can talk about an activity that has been running up to now and still shows.
teach.why_it_matters: It answers how long you have been doing something, and it explains the state you or a place are in without your having to name the state.
teach.meaning: This form points at the activity rather than at anything the activity produced. It says something has been going on across a stretch reaching up to this moment, and it very often exists to explain something the listener can see: the mud on the boots, the empty shelf, the tiredness. It makes no promise that the activity is finished, and quite often the whole point is that it is not.

notes: Three parts and all three are needed: the helper, been, and the -ing form
've been and 's been in speech, and both are short enough to disappear entirely
Verbs about states rather than activities refuse this form: know, own, belong, mean
form.negative: haven't been + the -ing form: I haven't been sleeping properly.
form.question: How long have you been + the -ing form ...?

marks.label: and runs all the way along here
which is why things look like this

spec.caption: The arrow is the activity. The mark at the end is the state it has left behind, and that state is usually why anybody said it.

worked_example.sentence: The team have been sampling the estuary since first light, which is why the boat is filthy.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence is about the work itself and the mess it made, not about a finished set of samples. Nobody is counting anything here.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Have sampled would put a finished set of samples on the table and leave the state of the boat out of the sentence entirely.

notice_set.sentence: Idris has been repainting the survey hut.
notice_set.question: Is the hut finished?
notice_set.why: The form points at the work rather than at a result, so whether it is done is simply not part of the claim.

notice_set.sentence: Idris has repainted the survey hut.
notice_set.question: Is the hut finished?
notice_set.why: Without been and the -ing, the sentence hands you the finished hut and says nothing about the afternoon that produced it.

notice_set.sentence: The pump has been running since Tuesday.
notice_set.question: Is it running at this moment?
notice_set.why: The activity is drawn as a line reaching the present moment, and nothing in the sentence cuts it off before then.

notice_set.sentence: You've been working outside, haven't you?
notice_set.question: How does the speaker know?
options: they can see the result on the person
notice_set.why: This is the form's commonest job: reading backwards from a state you can see to the activity that caused it.

notice_set.sentence: We have been waiting for the results for three weeks.
notice_set.question: Have the results come?
notice_set.why: The waiting is drawn as still running, and waiting that is still running has nothing at the end of it yet.

teach.rule_line: Use it for the activity itself, running up to now and often still going.
teach.false_rule: That it simply means for a long time. A three-minute activity takes it perfectly well when the activity is the thing you are pointing at.

errors.wrong: I have been knowing the family since I was small.
errors.right: I have known the family since I was small.
errors.why_it_happens: The stretch really does run up to now, and this is the form that draws a stretch, so it is a reasonable guess. Knowing is not an activity anyone performs, so English refuses to view it as one.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: have been knowing becomes have known.

errors.wrong: The clinic has been treating four hundred patients this month.
errors.right: The clinic has treated four hundred patients this month.
errors.why_it_happens: A counted total is a result, and this form is not looking at results. The number makes the sentence sound like a report while the verb is still pointing at the activity behind it.

points.title: Choosing between pointing at the finished thing and pointing at the doing

teach.can_do: I can choose between pointing at a finished result and pointing at the activity behind it.
teach.why_it_matters: Both forms are correct English and they answer different questions. The wrong one tells your listener the job is finished when it is not, or the reverse.
teach.meaning: Both forms reach from an earlier moment up to now, and when they arrive they look at different things. The simple form looks at what the activity produced: the finished thing, the total, the number done. The continuous looks at the activity itself: how long it has run, whether it is still going, and what state it has left everything in. Ask what you are pointing at and the choice makes itself.

form.pattern: simple: have / has + third form. continuous: have / has been + the -ing form
notes: A counted result pushes you towards the simple: I have sent four emails
A length, or an explanation of how things look, pushes you towards the continuous: I have been sending emails since eight
State verbs have no continuous at all, so the choice never arises with know, own, belong or mean
form.negative: haven't + third form for the result; haven't been + the -ing form for the activity.
form.question: How much have you done? asks for the simple. What have you been doing? asks for the continuous.

left.role: the simple: look at what came out of it

right.role: the continuous: look at the doing and the state it left

teach.rule_line: Point at the result with the simple; point at the doing with the continuous.
teach.false_rule: That the continuous means unfinished and the simple means finished. The continuous does not say either way. It is simply not looking at that.

contrast.question: Am I pointing at what is done, or at the doing?

fork.answer: At what is done: a result, a total, a number, a finished thing
fork.selects: the simple, as in have marked

fork.answer: At the doing: how long it ran, whether it is still going, why things look like this
fork.selects: the continuous, as in have been marking

a.means: Every essay is done and the pile is ready to hand back.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose has been marking. Your reader now expects an unfinished pile and asks how far you got. If every essay is done, the simple form says so and stops there.

edge_case.text: With live, work and study the two forms mean almost exactly the same thing and nobody will notice which you chose. Verbs about states, like know, own and belong, refuse the continuous outright, and that is a rule rather than a preference.

contrast.stronger_test: Try dropping a number into the sentence. If a count sits comfortably, you are in the simple. The continuous does not want counting; it wants a length.
